newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taipei entertainment joints rally against sex bust.
newsitem.headline: Taipei entertainment joints rally against sex bust.

text.p: Some 2,000 entertainment centre owners and workers besieged Taipei's city council on Thursday in protest against what they called a poorly targeted crackdown on Taiwan's flourishing but largely illegal sex industry.
"I have to live!" some demonstrators shouted outside the council headquarters while carrying white banners reading: "Give me back my innocence."
The demonstrators claimed Taipei police had mistaken their legitimate businesses for illegal sex parlours, the target of the city government's high-profile "war on prostitution".
State television estimated the number of protesters at 2,000.
Nearly 300 entertainment centres have been raided and closed in the past week in Mayor Chen Shui-bian's drive to rid Taipei of all "prostitution-related establishments."
Opponents of the crackdown accuse the police of carrying out the raids indiscriminately and of forcing even clean establishments to close.
"We wouldn't expose ourselves in broad daylight if we are actually running sex businesses," said Lin Chun-hsiung, head of Taiwan's Association of Barber Shops.
"It is not fair that people like us who provide legitimate entertainment with legal licences have to be forced out of work," Lin said.
Many of Taiwans thousands of barber shops are thinly disguised brothels or massage parlours that provide a full range of sex services, many of them illegal.
Yet some are legitimate businesses that offer hair styling, legal massages and non-sexual escort services -- making it hard for police to distinguish between valid commerce and vice.
Some of the protesters said their businesses offered nothing but hair styling.
Lin said the demonstrators have delivered a protest letter to the city council.
"We support the government's effort to crack down on prostitution, but we don't support the government driving innocent people out of business," he said.
Only a handful of Taiwan's thousands of call girls are licensed prostitutes.
Mayor Chen said he would not relent. "We will not compromise under any petition," the populist mayor said on state television.
Chen, who in 1994 became the first opposition party member elected Taipei mayor, has made a priority of ridding the city of its notorious red-light districts.
Prostitution has exploded alongside Taiwan's economic boom in recent years, with businessmen routinely taking male clients to sex parlours after work to build personal networks.
Taipei prostitutes reportedly can earn up to T$2 million (US$72,700) a month.
